title: HTTP vs gRPC streaming / chunking: field notes and microbenchmarks
body:
Summary:

Quick notes from a focused run comparing HTTP streaming (chunked responses + HTTP/2) to gRPC server-side streaming for small-to-medium token bursts. Goal was to isolate networking/transport overheads and backpressure behavior when the runtime emits tokens in small increments (1-64 tokens per flush). We also measured the delta when Envoy proxy sits between clients and the runtime.

Why this matters:
- Our runtime uses fine-grained token emission to support low-latency streaming for chat features. Small writes can cause non-obvious overhead at the kernel and proxy layers.
- Quantifying the tradeoffs helps Decide defaults for flush frequency / chunk size and whether customers should prefer gRPC or HTTP/2 for their integration.

Experiment goals:
- Measure P50/P95/P99 latency per token and end-to-end response completion time for identical service logic across transports.
- Measure CPU overhead on server for different flush sizes.
- Observe backpressure behavior: does the runtime stall when client consumes slowly? Do proxies introduce queueing that affects tail latency?
- Quick sanity check of HTTP/1.1 chunked (with TCP_NODELAY vs default), HTTP/2 (h2), and gRPC (http2-based) with and without Envoy.

Testbed and config:
- Server: 8 vCPU, 1xA10G-like GPU (mocked inference service that emits tokens per configured flush), Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.x, tuned tcp_mem default.
- Client: colocated in same AZ for baseline; remote (cross-AZ) for one run.
- Proxy: Envoy v1.30 with default HTTP/2 settings; one run with http/1.1 to test translation cost.
- Workload generator: custom bench harness (bench/network_streaming_runner.py) - uses grpcio and httpx for HTTP/2 tests; configurable flush sizes, concurrency, and delay between client reads.
- Token sizes: 10B token payload (simple JSON per token), simulated CPU cost per token kept constant to isolate networking.
- Flush sizes: 1 token, 4 tokens, 16 tokens, 64 tokens. Also a batched non-streaming baseline that returns entire response at once.

Commands used (examples):
- HTTP/2: httpx.AsyncClient(http2=True); curl --http2-prior-knowledge --no-buffer 
- gRPC: grpc-stub with server streaming; client reads stream.as_completed()
- Envoy: simple listener to upstream mapping with http2 on both sides; logs at debug for flow control windows.

Metrics collected:
- client-per-token-latency-ms (time from send request to receive token chunk)
- end-to-end completion time (first byte to last byte)
- server CPU% & system CPU (collected via top/collectl)
- socket-level retransmits and send/recv queue depths (ss, netstat, proc/net/dev)
- connection-level flow-control events from Envoy logs (when available)

Key results (summary):
- gRPC (server-streaming) gave the lowest 50/95 tail for 1-token flushes: P50 ~ 2.3ms, P95 ~ 9.1ms, P99 ~ 24ms (local AZ).
- HTTP/2 streaming (httpx/curl prior-knowledge) had slightly higher tails: P50 ~ 3.8ms, P95 ~ 12.7ms, P99 ~ 36ms for 1-token flushes.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked with TCP_NODELAY enabled was comparable to HTTP/2 for P50 but worse at P95/P99 due to head-of-line blocking in some cases.
- Envoy in the middle added 0.8-2.4ms median overhead and amplified tail: with Envoy P99 moved from ~24ms to ~47ms for gRPC 1-token flush runs in our environment.
- Increasing flush size reduces networking overhead but increases first-token latency (application-level): moving from 1->16 tokens reduced CPU overhead by ~18% and reduced P95 by ~35% but increased time-to-first-token by ~10-30ms depending on base token emission rate.
- Server CPU: small flush sizes increase syscalls and user->kernel transitions. Measured sys CPU increase of ~12% for 1-token flush vs batched, and 6% for 4-token flush.

Representative numbers (local AZ, single client, single connection):
- gRPC, flush=1 -> P50 2.3 ms, P95 9.1 ms, P99 24.0 ms, total completion 420 ms (for 100 tokens), server CPU 41%
- HTTP/2, flush=1 -> P50 3.8 ms, P95 12.7 ms, P99 36.0 ms, total completion 438 ms, server CPU 44%
- HTTP/1.1 chunked, flush=1 -> P50 3.6 ms, P95 17.8 ms, P99 65.2 ms, total 460 ms, server CPU 48%
- gRPC, flush=16 -> P50 6.8 ms (first token), P95 11.2 ms (subsequent tokens), P99 20.8 ms, total completion 360 ms, server CPU 34%
- Batched (no streaming) -> first byte 120 ms, P95 of delivery 120-130 ms, server CPU 29%

Observations and likely causes:
- Flow control interaction: gRPC's framing and client libraries appear to be more efficient at incremental reads; the runtime saw fewer pending bytes on socket with gRPC vs raw chunked HTTP/1.1, reducing kernel copy overhead.
- Envoy behavior: Envoy introduces an internal buffer between upstream and downstream; small writes from upstream get coalesced but also buffered if downstream hasn't consumed. Envoy's connection pool/idle timeout and HTTP/2 window sizing caused bursts to be delayed while watermarks adjust.
- TCP_NODELAY: enabling TCP_NODELAY reduced latency for 1-token flushes in HTTP/1.1 but increased packet-per-token overhead leading to higher CPU. The tradeoff looks unfavorable for high-concurrency cases.
- Kernel-level batching: when multiple small writes are coalesced into single TCP segments, P50 improves but P99 can still suffer due to delayed ACKs or Nagle interactions if not explicitly disabled.

Backpressure experiments (slow client read):
- Setup: client intentionally sleeps 10ms between reads to simulate slow consumer.
- gRPC: server-side send calls started to block only after ~64KB of unacked data; client-side observed smooth slowdown but no spike in tail beyond expected.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked: server send calls returned EAGAIN earlier with default socket buffer sizes; runtime saw send loop stalls and increased context switches.
- Envoy in the middle: made backpressure effects worse because it buffers a few KBs and then exerts backpressure on upstream only once its internal watermarks hit. This created a delayed, larger stall event on the server side (i.e., not gradual).

Actionable takeaways:
1) For streaming-first experiences where token-at-a-time latency matters (chat UX), recommend gRPC server-streaming as the default SDK transport for enterprise customers when using the dedicated/private offering. It provides lower tail and cleaner backpressure behavior in our tests.
2) For hosted HTTP clients (web browsers) where gRPC-web isn't an option, prefer HTTP/2 streaming and configure runtime defaults to emit in small batches (e.g., 4 tokens) instead of 1 token. This balances latency and CPU.
3) If customers must use HTTP/1.1 chunked, provide clear guidance: enable TCP_NODELAY only when low concurrency and accept higher CPU; otherwise instruct to use slightly larger flush sizes (16 tokens) to avoid syscall storms.
4) Add default Envoy tuning in our reference proxy config to reduce tail amplification: increase per-connection HTTP/2 initial window and lower upstream buffer watermarks, and add explicit small_write_coalescing when possible. Document tradeoffs.
5) In the runtime, expose a simple knob: flush_token_count with sensible defaults per deployment type (hosted/dedicated/private).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Multi-client scenarios at higher QPS: these tests are single-connection. Need to scale to 50-200 concurrent streams and observe connection-level behavior (window updates, cross-talk).
- Evaluate gRPC-web (Envoy proxy path) for browser clients: does translating gRPC-web->gRPC amplify overhead similarly to Envoy h2->h2 path?
- Investigate a lib-level optimization to coalesce small writes into a single writev call per event loop tick to reduce syscalls while preserving low time-to-first-token.
- Test with realistic token sizes (varying from 5 bytes -> 200 bytes) and random jitter in emission to reflect model KV cache behavior.

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Re-run with 200 concurrent streams across 4 client VMs and attach pcap for a tail case where Envoy caused 200ms stall.
- Open a follow-up PR to our reference-envoy-config repo with suggested watermarks (PR draft created: see linked_artifacts).
- Add support in bench harness to record socket-level cwnd/rcv_space snapshots periodically.
- Share this note with Console team (Lena) for flags UI so customers can set flush_token_count in the console.

Experimental artifacts & pointers:
- bench harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/tree/main/networking
- small write coalescing PoC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/879
- related JIRA: JIRA-ISSUE-1421 (envoy tail investigation)

Conclusions (short):
- gRPC wins in tail and backpressure stability for token-at-a-time streaming.
- HTTP/2 is acceptable and simpler for browser/backward compat but requires tuning and slightly larger flush batches.
- Envoy is convenient but amplifies tail behavior unless tuned; default configs currently hurt streaming latency.

If we want to be conservative in product defaults: choose gRPC for SDKs, HTTP/2 for browser flows with flush=4 default, and update docs/console with guidance and proxy tuning.

End of notes.
